## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pūraḷāsa Sutta* (Snp 3.4), situated in the Mahāvagga of the *Suttanipāta*, is also known as the *Sundarikabhāradvāja Sutta* [SuttaCentral; Norman 1997-2001; Saddhatissa 2013]. The title refers to the *pūraḷāsa* (Sanskrit *puroḍāśa*), the oblation or sacrificial cake used in Brahmanical rites [Saddhatissa 2013]. In the discourse, the brahman Sundarika-Bhāradvāja questions the Buddha to ascertain whether he deserves to receive the remnants of his sacrificial offering [SuttaCentral; Saddhatissa 2013]. When the brahman initiates their encounter by inquiring into the Buddha's caste according to Brahmanical social convention, the Buddha critiques the relevance of caste origins, setting forth instead the moral and spiritual attributes that truly define a sage deserving of offerings [Obeyesekere; Anderson and Smith 1913]. Multiple stanzas culminate in the refrain affirming that one endowed with spiritual purity and wisdom is worthy of the sacrificial cake (*tathāgato arahati pūraḷāsam*) [Anderson and Smith 1913; Norman 1997-2001]. Convinced by the teaching, the brahman renounces household life and attains arahantship [Saddhatissa 2013].
SuttaCentral identifies a direct passage-level parallel in the Saṁyutta Nikāya's *Sundarikasutta* (SN 7.9), alongside related discourses involving the Bhāradvāja lineage, such as the *Kasibhāradvāja Sutta* (Snp 1.4; SN 7.11) and *Aggikasutta* (SN 7.8) [SuttaCentral]. Computational reuse analysis by DharmaNexus strongly confirms this distribution, recording its heaviest internal correspondence with the *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7, sharing substantial parallel text with SN 7.9), followed by the commentary *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Māgha Sutta* (Snp 3.5), and recurring formulaic passages shared across the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* and *Majjhima Nikāya* [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language parallels and alignments exist with the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99 and T 100) and *Ekottarikāgama* (T 125), as well as thematic verse parallels in the *Udānavarga* (*Brāhmaṇavarga*) attested in Sanskrit manuscripts and Tibetan versions (D0326, D4099), while the text is also cited in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.5.9) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
